Summary

The Cornerstone EEIO model is updated annually and versioned with the year of the release, so Cornerstone EEIO 2026 is released in 2026 and the 2027 version will be released in 2027. Every year, the releases will be publicly available in October. Each release publishes emission factors covering 405 sectors across 148 countries, 21 regions and one global average. To download the latest version, check out 

Zenodo.
The release includes one Excel workbook that contains: a cover, a data dictionary, a producer-price tab and a purchaser-price tab for each year the data is available for, and five auxiliary tabs.

hierarchy.lvl3: Cover
Cover

records.content:
The first tab introduces the dataset and the release details:

Description: cradle-to-gate greenhouse gas emission factors in kg CO₂e per USD, by good or service, location and year, in producer and purchaser price. Prices are in current-year dollars, so the dollar year matches the data year.

Coverage: 148 countries and 21 regions, and 405 categories of goods and services (government services are not covered). The total and each gas (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs, NF₃, SF₆) are given in CO₂e, annually from 2018 to 2026.

Publisher and license: Cornerstone Sustainability Data Initiative, under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license.

Below these details, the cover lists every other tab with a one-line description and points readers to the data dictionary and the model documentation.

hierarchy.lvl3: Producer and purchaser price tabs
Producer and purchaser price tabs

records.content:
There are two tabs for each year, with identical layouts: {YEAR}PRO for producer prices and {YEAR}PUR for purchaser prices. The producer price is the cost to the producer plus their profits and taxes paid. The purchaser price adds the value of sales and distribution. Read more about how to choose between purchaser and producer prices in 

How-to 2: Purchaser vs. producer price, and margins.

Each row is one sector in one location, and the columns are:

Column

Meaning

Code

Good or service code, based on the BEA input-output commodity codes, which derive from NAICS. There are 405 categories.

Name

Name of the good or service.

Location

A UN three-letter country code, with additions for multi-country regions.

Total GHGs

Sum of all greenhouse gases, in kg CO₂e per USD.

CO2

Carbon dioxide, in kg CO₂e per USD.

CH4

Methane, in kg CO₂e per USD.

N2O

Nitrous oxide, in kg CO₂e per USD.

HFCs

Hydrofluorocarbons, in kg CO₂e per USD.

PFCs

Perfluorocarbons, in kg CO₂e per USD.

NF3

Nitrogen trifluoride, in kg CO₂e per USD.

SF6

Sulfur hexafluoride, in kg CO₂e per USD.

Values are in current-year dollars: a factor in a 2024 tab applies to spend in 2024 dollars.

hierarchy.lvl3: Auxiliary tabs
Auxiliary tabs

records.content:
The data dictionary and five other tabs support the data tabs. The data dictionary is the second tab in the workbook; the others follow the price tabs.

Tab

What it contains

Data Dictionary

Definitions of each field in the data tabs.

Exchange rates

Local currency units per US dollar for 148 countries: country code and name, currency, unit, and one column per year from 2018 to 2026. Rates come from Open Exchange Rates (

openexchangerates​.org) and are Cornerstone’s recommended rates for converting spend in local currency before applying the factors.

GWP

The 100-year global warming potentials from the IPCC AR6 that express each gas in CO₂e: CO₂ 1, CH₄ 27.9 (to confirm), N₂O 273, SF₆ 24,300 and NF₃ 17,400. HFCs and PFCs are already in CO₂e, so their factor is 1.

Cornerstone <> NAICS mapping

The correspondence between NAICS 2022 codes and Cornerstone codes: NAICS code and name, Cornerstone code and title, and a weight. When a NAICS industry is split across several Cornerstone codes, the weights show each share and add up to 1.

GoodsServices

The 405 sectors with their code, name and description. Cornerstone recommends using this description to map spend categories to emission factors.

Locations

Every location code and name used in the model: countries by their three-letter code, and regions.

The Cornerstone EEIO follows an annual update cycle. Every year we release a version named after the release year, so Cornerstone 2027 will be released in 2027. Releases are publicly available every October so companies can plan accordingly.

Starter definitions drawn from the site plan; team to review and extend. Terms defined here can be linked from any page with {term}`MRIO` and show a hover definition.

ABSR

Auto-Balanced Structural Reflection. The method that expands a country’s coarser IO table onto the model’s common sector schema, using U.S. structure as weights, while keeping the country’s accounts balanced.

Basic price

The amount a producer receives for a product, excluding taxes on products and including subsidies on products.

BACI

The CEPII database of bilateral international trade by product, used to split each country’s imports by country of origin.

Country tier

A group of countries modeled with the same level of detail and the same kinds of data sources: Tier 0, detailed annual IO tables (the United States); Tier 1, detailed periodic national IO tables; Tier 2, coarse multi-regional tables from FIGARO or ICIO; and Tier 3, no IO tables (a template built from other countries).

EEIO

Environmentally-extended input-output model. An input-output model of an economy with environmental data (here, greenhouse gas emissions) attached to each sector.

FIGARO

Full International and Global Accounts for Research in input-Output analysis. Multi-regional IO tables from Eurostat and the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre, used for many Tier 2 countries.

GWP

Global warming potential. The warming effect of 1 kg of a gas relative to 1 kg of CO₂ over a time horizon. The model uses AR6 values with a 100-year horizon.

Make/Use framework

IO tables that record which industries make which commodities (Make, or supply) and which commodities each industry and final user buys (Use).

Margins

The trade and transport costs added between the producer and the buyer: transport, wholesale, and retail.

MRIO

Multi-regional input-output model. Country IO tables linked into one global system through international trade.

ICIO

The OECD Inter-Country Input-Output tables, used for Tier 2 countries not covered by FIGARO.

Producer price

The basic price plus taxes on products, less subsidies on products, excluding margins.

Purchaser price

The price the buyer pays: the producer price plus trade and transport margins. The published factors are per dollar of purchaser price.

RAS

An iterative method that scales the rows and columns of a table until it matches known row and column totals.

Redefinitions

Adjustments that move secondary products (and their inputs) to the industry where they are the primary product.

Structural reflection

Using a detailed table’s structure (here, the U.S. tables) as weights to split a coarser table into finer sectors.

Summary

This table summarizes all the data and methodology changes behind Cornerstone EEIO 2026, compared to both USEEIO v1.4 and CEDA 2025.

Type of change

Category

What changed?

Data update

US data

Updated the U.S. GHG emissions data (totals and by sector) released by the University of Maryland Greenhouse Gas Inventory and Analysis (UMD GHGIA) 

(link) from 2023 to 2024.

Data update

UK data

Updated the UK IO tables released by the U.K. Office for National Statistics 

(link) from 2022 to 2023, incorporating the most recent benchmark IO tables.

Updated the U.K. GHG emissions data released by the U.K. Office for National Statistics 

(link) from 2022 to 2023, incorporating the most recent benchmark IO tables.

Data update

China data

Updated the China IO tables released by the National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBS) 

(link) from 2020 to 2023, incorporating the most recent benchmark IO tables.

Updated the China GHG emissions data released by Our World in Data (OWID) 

(link), Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) 

(link), and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR) 

(link) from 2020 to 2023, incorporating the most recent benchmark IO tables.

Data update

Europe & other global data

Updated the tier 2 country IO tables using Eurostat’s Full International and Global Accounts for Research in Input-Output Analysis (FIGARO) 

(link) for 2023 data where available and otherwise to 2020 OECD IO tables 

(link).

Updated the tier 2 country emissions data using FIGARO’s 2023 data 

(link) where available and otherwise to 2020 OECD IO tables 

(link).

Data update

Global trade data

Updated global trade data released by the United Nations Comtrade (BACI) 

(link) from 2023 to 2024.

Global trade data is supplemented with FIGARO trade data 

(link) to fill gaps in BACI data.

Methodology improvements

Model reconciliation

USEEIO and CEDA teams reviewed 18 differences between the models for the US and either adopted one of the model’s approaches or proposed an improvement. The differences can be categorized into 3 types: sectors schema, treatment of economic data and GHG attribution. For details on the differences, see the 

model reconciliation section below.

Methodology improvements

Auto-balancing structural reflection (ABSR)

Improved disaggregation of non-US economic data into detailed sectors using a new block scaling method.

Methodology improvements

US nowcasting and facility reported data

Estimated detailed 2024 US IO tables from primary sources from 2017 to 2024, replicating the tables produced by the BEA.

Used facility reported data to allocate emissions of manufacturing sectors, instead of survey data.

Methodology improvements

Bug fixes

Corrected errors in HS mapping.

Corrected double application of AR5 to AR6 conversion.

Corrected loading of the UK IO table.

Methodology improvements

Benchmark informed improvements

Leveraged third-party benchmark data created with ~1,000 data sources to review key sectors that drive ~50% of global emissions, producing one of three outcomes: benchmark improvements, model improvements or documentation of known discrepancies. More on why we benchmark in 

Why we benchmark.

The USEEIO and the US portion of CEDA had 18 methodological differences. Cornerstone EEIO adopted either one of the approaches for each difference or improved the approach. For more details on each topic, see our open discussions on 

GitHub.

Cornerstone EEIO 2026 - RC

Summary

The Cornerstone EEIO 2026 - RC (Release Candidate) is the first stage of a phased approach to releasing the Cornerstone EEIO 2026 model, the successor of USEEIO and CEDA. It is a global environmentally-extended input-output (EEIO) model that produces spend-based emission factors, in kg CO₂e per USD for 405 sectors across 148 countries, plus 21 regional averages and one global average. It uses 2024 as the base year and is available to use for 2024, 2025 and 2026 measurements.

This release candidate will be superseded in December by the release of the Cornerstone EEIO 2026 final version, which will include a time series from 2017 to 2026.

Download this release on 

Zenodo here.

Why have a Release Candidate?

2026 is an unprecedented year of development because it is the first time we are combining CEDA and USEEIO into one model and also the first time we are releasing a time series. The intention behind having a two phased approach to the release is to give companies additional time for impact assessments on their most recent year of measurements, while the time series is under development. This enables companies to understand footprint changes before applying the time series.

Will there be any changes for years 2024 to 2026 once the time series is released?

We do not foresee significant changes, but some sector-country combinations could be impacted by improvements driven from the time series model development. Users should consider this version as a release candidate and wait for the final 2026 version of this model that will be released in early December for reporting and rebaselining purposes.

What to expect from the time series?

The time series (2017-2026) will use the same methodology for all years and only change the underlying data that represents each country’s economic structure and emissions data. For example, in the US each year of the dataset will use the US electricity grid emissivity for each year, capturing any decarbonization on this sector year over year.

This is the first time that either USEEIO or CEDA releases a time series built this way. In the past CEDA has released a time series built with inflation adjustments for years prior and after the base year. Moving forward the Cornerstone EEIO will only apply inflation adjustments to the years after the base year, for which there is no reported data (e.g. 2025 and 2026 are inflation adjusted from the 2024 base year).

To learn more about the methodology behind Cornerstone EEIO refer to 

the IO model and 

the GHG extension.

Cornerstone EEIO 2026 combines USEEIO’s detailed picture of the US economy with CEDA’s global coverage and trade modeling, representing a step change improvement to both models.

Three groups of improvements sit behind the changes.

A more current picture of the US economy that accounts for imports. US input-output tables are rebuilt for every year from 2017 to 2024, manufacturing uses facility-reported emissions, and imports are modeled where they are made.

Newer data for Europe, the UK and China, and better gap-filling for the rest. Europe moves from the OECD’s ICIO tables to Eurostat’s FIGARO (through 2023). China moves to the latest National Bureau of Statistics tables (through 2023), with more sectors. Countries without data are filled with the auto-balanced structural reflection method.

A validation process that feeds back into the model. Third-party benchmarks review the sectors behind about 50% of global emissions. Gaps are traced and fixed in the data or the method and documented when unresolved.

Together these make the 2017–2026 time series possible.
They translate real world changes to corporate footprints. Three examples show how:

hierarchy.lvl3: New data for China
New data for China

records.content:
Cornerstone adopts the most recent economic data released by the Chinese National Bureau of Statistics (2023 vs. 2020), which reflects methodology changes, changes in the economic structure, and sector-specific decarbonization.

For example, China’s battery factor rises by ~30% driven by a change in the composition of battery production in China. From 2020 to 2023, battery production more than tripled, but more importantly it shifted to require more Lithium-ion and less Lead-acid as inputs. This is because the majority of the market growth in batteries are in EVs and grid storage that require lithium-ion. Lithium-ion needs lithium chemicals and power-hungry cell factories, being more carbon intensive per dollar than lead-acid batteries, driving the emission factor up.



Figure 1:China battery production, 2020 and 2023. Output in GWh. The split by battery type is approximate. Sources: NBS input-output tables 2020 and 2023; MIIT; China lead-acid battery industry statistics.

hierarchy.lvl3: New data for Europe
New data for Europe

records.content:
Cornerstone adopts the most recent release of FIGARO, Eurostat’s official input-output and emissions dataset. FIGARO is more granular than the OECD dataset for Europe, is available as a time series through 2023, and is updated every year, matching Cornerstone’s release cadence.

This data update lowers European factors by about 4% in median. The most significant change is in electricity factors, which fall in every EU country. This change is driven by an increase in renewable energy and by an increase in energy prices due to the gas-supply shocks the Ukraine war has caused in Europe. For example, Germany’s power factor fell by 60%, as renewables grew from 35% to over 50% of generation and wholesale power prices more than doubled.



Figure 2:Germany’s power emission factor falls by 60%. About 25% of the change comes from a cleaner grid, as renewables grew from 35% to over 50% of generation, and about 75% from higher prices, as wholesale power prices more than doubled, from about €44 to €95 per MWh. Sources: Ember, Öko-Institut, SMARD, Vattenfall.

hierarchy.lvl3: Incorporation of imports in the US
Incorporation of imports in the US

records.content:
USEEIO treated the US as a closed economy: every product used in the US was assumed to be made in the US. Cornerstone uses trade data to model each import in the country that produced it. Many imports come from more emissions-intensive economies such as China and India, so US factors tend to rise by 10 to 30% on average. This is the main upward pressure and the main reason for the change for USEEIO users. One example is light trucks and utility vehicles. The US factor rises by ~24%, mostly because many of their components are now modeled as imports from the countries that make them. Public data suggests that about 60% of the components of a US-assembled light truck are imported, with Mexico the largest source, followed by Europe and Canada (see 

Figure 3).



Figure 3:Estimated origin of the components of a US-assembled light truck. Sources: 

NHTSA AALA parts content data; 

International Trade Administration data as reported by MNI (March 2025).

hierarchy.lvl3: Auto-balanced structural reflection (ABSR)
hierarchy.lvl2: What drives the change for CEDA users

hierarchy.lvl3: Auto-balanced structural reflection (ABSR)
hierarchy.lvl2: What drives the change for CEDA users

records.content:
Structural reflection is the method CEDA uses to give every country the same sectors. ABSR improves it. It achieves two goals that are hard to deliver together in a global model:

All countries share the same 405 sectors, so emission factors compare like for like.

Each economy balances production and consumption, in both money and emissions.

Cornerstone uses benchmark data built from about 1,000 sources to review the key sectors that drive about 50% of global emissions. Each review ends in one of three outcomes:

Sharper benchmark. Scope and price assumptions are aligned, so the external reference is directly comparable to the model.

Model improvement. The gap is traced to a data source or an allocation method, and fixed with more data or a corrected implementation.

Known discrepancy. The difference is documented, because of a limitation in how the model is built or a gap in the data.

About 70% of country-sector pairs with a verified benchmark are within 25% of it. 21% are 25–50% apart and 10% are 50% or more apart.

Outcome

Example

Gap before and after

Sharper benchmark

US electricity: the benchmark covered only private utilities, while the model also includes state and local utilities. Aligning scope gives a benchmark of 2.37 against the model’s 2.44 kg CO₂e per USD.

15% to 3%

Model improvement

Brazil dairy: the model was allocating methane from beef to dairy for lack of country-specific data. Brazil’s national accounts of emissions and output fixed it.

51% to 5%

Known discrepancy

US oil and gas: the benchmark roughly doubles methane using aerial and satellite measurements. The model uses the EPA inventory, as for every other sector. Resolving this needs more research.

22% (stays)

records.content:
The USEEIO and CEDA teams reviewed 18 differences between the two models for the US. For each, they adopted one model’s approach or proposed an improvement. The differences can be categorized into 3 types: sectors schema, treatment of economic data and GHG attribution. For details on the differences, see the 

model reconciliation section of the change log.

One example of these differences is using the BEA after redefinition input output tables instead of the before redefinition tables. A detailed explanation of why this is the approach can be found on GitHub 

here.

hierarchy.lvl3: Nowcasting and facility-reported data
hierarchy.lvl2: What drives the change for USEEIO users

hierarchy.lvl3: Nowcasting and facility-reported data
hierarchy.lvl2: What drives the change for USEEIO users

records.content:
BEA publishes detailed (about 400-sector) US input-output tables only every 10 years, with a five-year lag. The latest is for 2017. Nowcasting rebuilds these tables for every year from 2017 to 2024, in BEA’s own structure, using the same official statistics BEA uses. This methodology improvement enables building the time series and providing a more current picture of the US economy. More than 50% of the economic data behind the factors is now backed by reported annual data, beyond inflation adjustments.

Cornerstone EEIO also uses facility-level reported emissions data from the US EPA’s Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) where most of the facilities in a sector report them, in place of using estimates based on 4-yr frequency fuel use data. The 2024 data includes 6,127 facility reports across 84 industries. This improvement provides a more accurate picture of the US economy. For example, the US sector emissions now match the totals reported across 87 cement plants (61 MT) in 2024. USEEIO undercounted them by ~20%, driving an increase in emission factors in kg CO₂e/USD.



Figure 4:Cement sector emission factor, USEEIO v1.4 and Cornerstone 2026. In kg CO₂e per USD.
